title_original: WhiteWall CEO Petra Felgen: “AI Should Support the Photographer’s Creative Work, Not Reinterpret It”

blocks.text: Mounting, finishing, frames made to measure in its own workshop: since Alexander Nieswandt founded it in 2007, WhiteWall has produced everything in a lab of more than 10,000 square meters in Frechen, near Cologne, from which prints ship to more than 60 countries. A subsidiary of the CEWE group and the winner of eight TIPA World Awards, the company employs more than 200 people and runs four stores in Germany (Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Munich and Berlin), as well as sales spaces inside LUMAS galleries in New York, Miami, Zurich and Vienna. In the second quarter of 2026, its leadership changed: Petra Felgen, previously Managing Director of CEWE Ltd. for the United Kingdom and Ireland, succeeded Thomas Alscheid, who had held the post for seven years, while the founder continues to oversee production. Meanwhile, the lab has expanded its online configurator: SuperResolution , which uses AI to enlarge files whose resolution is too low, ultraHD sharpening, automatic color and contrast optimization, and Frame Finder , an assistant that analyzes an image and recommends three frames from more than 100 profiles. A new 3D view also lets customers visualize several pieces on the same wall. All of which raises a basic question for photographers: how far can a lab go in intervening on an image?
Alexander Nieswandt remains in charge of production. How do you two split decisions, and who has the final word?

Alexander and I bring different but complementary strengths to WhiteWall. As the company’s founder, he has an exceptional depth of knowledge of our production processes and technical expertise, and he continues to play a key role in this area. As CEO, I am responsible for the overall strategic direction and performance of WhiteWall, including setting priorities and making decisions that shape the company’s future. Many important decisions benefit from close collaboration, but we each have clearly defined responsibilities. Ultimately, I carry responsibility for the overall direction of the business.

blocks.text: SuperResolution “adds missing details” using AI. When does improving a file become inventing an image?

There is an important distinction between enhancing an image for printing and altering it in a way that changes its appearance or even its message. We are very conscious of that boundary, and it is one we do not cross with SuperResolution. We carried out extensive testing, always from a photographer’s perspective: how can we achieve the best possible print quality while preserving the original image? This helped us identify the right technology and settings to increase resolution without changing the character or content of the photograph. Our aim is not to generate new image elements or introduce details that were never part of the original. Instead, the technology identifies and enhances existing image information. For us, the principle is clear: AI should support the photographer’s creative work, not reinterpret it.
Why are the AI optimization tools switched on by default rather than opt-in?

In most cases, our customers — particularly professional photographers and photography enthusiasts — upload files with enough resolution, often more than enough, for the selected print size. In these instances, SuperResolution is not applied, as the system checks the available resolution against the chosen print dimensions. However, a file may not have sufficient resolution because of a crop, an older digital file or a lower-resolution backup when the original is no longer available. We want customers to achieve the best possible print quality in these cases, too. That is why we decided to enable the feature by default. At the same time, the setting is clearly visible, and customers can switch it on or off and save their preference for future orders. Some photographers prefer to leave their images entirely untouched, and we fully respect that.

blocks.text: Is SuperResolution built in-house, within CEWE, or on third-party models? And are customers’ files used to train it?

We work with a specialized technology partner who provides the underlying AI technology for image enhancement and upscaling. However, a substantial part of the development took place in-house: our team tested a wide range of images from our own image pool to determine the optimal parameters for our printing processes. Customers’ images are not used to train the AI models. Feedback from customers and discussions with the photographers we work closely with also played an important role.

blocks.text: What does Frame Finder actually analyze in an image, and how do its picks compare with those of your framers in Frechen?

Frame Finder analyzes a photograph in much the same way an experienced framer would, looking at four key aspects: color, subject and mood, materials and textures, and composition. It identifies dominant colors, their intensity and temperature, and whether an image is in color, black and white or toned. It recognizes whether it is a portrait, a landscape, an architectural photograph or a fine art image, and considers the positioning of the subject, negative space and elements extending to the edges. An image with prominent steel and glass elements, for instance, might work particularly well with an aluminum frame. If important elements extend right to the edge, a floater frame may be less suitable, as the surrounding shadow gap could interrupt the composition. Frame Finder then suggests three framing options and explains why each might work. The concept is inspired by our team, who combine these principles with years of hands-on experience, deep knowledge of materials and an understanding of each customer’s preferences.
Will prints enlarged with AI be labeled as such, for galleries and collectors? Are you considering a standard like C2PA, which certifies the provenance of images?

We use the AI-upscaled image exclusively for production. The enhanced file is stored internally for printing purposes only and deleted afterwards. We do not share it with anyone outside WhiteWall, including the customer who ordered the print. C2PA is an important technology for verifying the authenticity and provenance of digital images, but as this file is never distributed, applying the standard to it would not serve a practical purpose. We also do not physically label prints produced using AI-based upscaling.

blocks.text: As more of the printer’s craft moves into software, how do you see lab jobs evolving over the next five years?

I see technology and craftsmanship as complementary rather than competing forces. Software and automation can take over increasingly complex technical tasks and improve consistency, but they do not replace the experience, judgment and attention to detail that are essential to producing outstanding prints. I expect roles in the lab to become increasingly specialized, with a stronger focus on technical expertise, quality control and the ability to work with new materials and processes. Understanding how digital files translate into physical prints will remain particularly important.

blocks.text: How do you keep a high-end, gallery-quality image while opening up to a much broader public?

For us, gallery-quality standards and reaching a broader audience are not contradictory. Our standards remain exactly the same, whether we are producing a print for an internationally renowned photographer, an ambitious amateur or someone who simply wants to give a personal photograph a special place in their home. The key is to make professional standards accessible without compromising on quality. Our online configurator guides customers through the range of materials, formats and finishes, while our teams in WhiteWall stores and our online customer service offer individual advice. Expanding our audience does not mean lowering our standards; it means making our expertise accessible to more people.
WhiteWall’s prints, frames and online tools are available at whitewall.com and in the company’s stores in Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Munich and Berlin.
